content.text: A document database doesn't enforce a schema by default, but your data still has one: it lives in every piece of code that reads it. Skipping modeling moves that schema from one declared place into many hidden ones, and skipping migrations means every reader must handle every old shape. Model around your access patterns, version your documents, and turn on the validation your database already offers.

The belief: NoSQL databases are schemaless, so you can skip data modeling and never migrate data.

It's half true, which is what makes it convincing. MongoDB's docs say documents in one collection aren't required to have the same fields or data types, and that you can add new fields without rewriting existing documents or running a schema migration. There's no
, no migration script in the pull request, and a prototype moves fast. Years of "rigid SQL versus flexible NoSQL" talks did the rest.
The schema moved into your code

Martin Fowler's slide title is blunt: "schemaless structures still have an implicit schema". His reason: "Any code that manipulates the data needs to make some assumptions about its structure, such as the name of fields." Microsoft's comparison of data store models puts it in two phrases: relational databases are schema on write, document stores are
. The database accepts any shape, and every reader decides what it means. The report in the test was a reader that assumed
. Fowler's slide finishes the thought: data that doesn't fit the
"will not be manipulated properly, leading to errors."
You still model, just around access patterns

Document modeling isn't optional; it's different. MongoDB calls it a core principle that data accessed together should be stored together, and advises planning the schema before production scale. Microsoft's Cosmos DB guide says data modeling in a schema-free database is "as important as ever." Embed related data when it's contained, one-to-few, read together, changes rarely and doesn't grow without bound. Reference it when it's one-to-many or many-to-many, changes often or is unbounded. Embedding a copy brings back the update problem normalization solves: the same guide accepts that if an author changes their name, every book document that embeds it needs an update. And references are weak: Cosmos DB has no foreign key constraints, so checking that a referenced document exists is up to your application or server-side code.

Old documents keep their old shape until something rewrites them. Fowler describes the usual technique: access code reads either the old or the new format and saves only the new one, so data migrates gradually, and the old-format code is removed once the migration is done. His conclusion: "Similar migration techniques are usually required with schemaless databases too, although flexible access code does help."
Most document stores can enforce a schema

MongoDB's schema validation applies JSON Schema rules to inserts and updates, and by default rejects any write that would produce an invalid document. Its docs recommend it for an established application with a defined data structure. The flexibility runs both ways: relational databases have schemaless corners too. In the test, a

How to apply it in your project

Give each collection one owner: a data access layer with typed models, a JSON Schema file, or both. Fowler suggests a clear data access layer and/or a predicate schema to reduce the problems of a hidden, implicit one.
List the reads and writes each screen and job performs, then decide what to embed and what to reference with the rules above. Watch for arrays that can grow without bound.

items.text: Schemaless means the database doesn't check the shape; the schema still exists in every reader.
A missing or renamed field doesn't fail on write: in the test, it silently removed 99.00 from a revenue total.
Document databases still need modeling, built around access patterns: embed what's read together and bounded, reference the rest.
Migrations don't disappear; they become gradual, and old shapes stay until you backfill them.
Write the schema down, version documents, and turn on validation once the shape is stable.
